title: Boeuf en Daube
subtitle: Provençal braised beef with olives and orange
excerpt: The Provençal version of beef stew: chunks of beef braised overnight with red wine, olives, orange peel, and herbes de Provence until the meat falls apart in a wine-dark, fragrant sauce. A long, gentle cook is the only technique required.

recipe.sourceNotes: Boeuf en daube (daube simply refers to the covered earthenware vessel called a daubière in which the stew was traditionally cooked) is the signature meat dish of Provence in southern France. It appears in Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse as a symbol of warmth, domesticity, and the civilising power of good food. The defining characteristics that distinguish it from other French beef braises are the Provençal aromatics: olives, orange peel, and herbes de Provence (thyme, bay, rosemary, and marjoram or oregano). The stew is traditionally marinated in wine overnight before cooking, which was originally intended to tenderise older, tougher beef; with modern butchery this step is optional but adds depth. The dish reheats excellently and is often eaten the day after cooking.

content.text: Use a cheap, full-bodied red wine; it will cook for hours and a fine wine would be wasted. The stew should barely simmer; at a proper daube temperature the surface just trembles. Any more and the beef fibres tighten and the sauce turns thin and metallic.

content.text: Season the beef. Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy casserole. Brown the pancetta, then remove. Brown the beef in batches over high heat until deeply coloured on all sides. Remove.

Cook the onion and carrot in the remaining fat for 5 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato puree. Cook for 1 minute. Pour in the wine and stock. Bring to a simmer, scraping up any browned bits. Return the beef and pancetta with the bay leaves, thyme, and orange peel.

Cover tightly and braise on the lowest possible heat for 2.5 to 3 hours, or in an oven at 150°C / fan 130°C / gas 2, until the beef is completely tender. In the last 30 minutes, add the olives. Remove the bay leaves and orange peel before serving over wide noodles or with crusty bread.
